sections.h2: Which city office sends the bill
sections.html:
The Collector of Revenue sends it, and the Assessor decides what the house is worth. St. Louis stands apart from any county, so these two City Hall offices do the jobs that a county treasurer and county assessor handle elsewhere in Missouri. Both work out of 1200 Market Street.

For valuation questions, the Assessor's real estate staff answer at (314) 622-4185 and assessor-real-estate@stlouis-mo.gov, in Room 120, weekdays from eight in the morning to five in the afternoon. Payments are taken in Room 109. The same Collector also bills personal property tax, earnings tax and water-refuse charges, so a house seller may hear from that office about more than one account.

The Collector tracks about 220,000 parcels, and the Assessor revalues them in odd-numbered years.

The city is home to an estimated 278,144 people, down 7.7% from the April 2020 base. Owners live in only 45.3% of homes, so rentals make up most of the housing stock. That matters if your property has a tenant. The median owner-reported home value is $197,500, median rent is $997 and median household income is $56,160. The city covers 61.74 square miles of land.

Owners with a mortgage report monthly costs near $1,487 in the middle, while those without a loan report $574. Set those figures beside the bill on your own parcel. A tax line that looks heavy next to them is a reason to prepare an appeal before May 1 arrives.

sections.h2: Due date, penalties and how to pay
sections.html:
Interest and a penalty begin on January 1. The Collector charges a single 2% penalty, then 2% interest each month, topping out at 18% for the year, and the interest keeps building each year until the balance is cleared. If more than one year is owed, the oldest year gets paid first.

Notices go out in November. Where a lender escrows the tax, the bill goes to the lender instead of you. If nothing shows up in your mailbox, the Assessor may hold an old address for you, or the deed may have changed hands after the bills were printed. Every bill can be viewed online. Address changes go through the Assessor in City Hall Room 114.

Ways to pay a St. Louis real estate tax bill
Payment optionWhereNotes
Online or phone appPayIt St. Louis accountWeb or mobile
In personRoom 109, Monday to FridayCurrent-year bills by card, cash, check, money order or cashier's check; delinquent bills cannot be paid by check
MailCollector of Revenue, PO Box 66877, St. Louis, MO 63166-6877Check, money order or cashier's check
Phone(314) 408-6887Card payment

Between mid-October and December 31, night deposit boxes at four Commerce Bank branches also accept payments. A pre-pay program lets owners deposit money toward later bills.

You have three stages. The informal stage opens May 1 and closes June 23. Send appeal@stlouis-mo.gov your parcel number or address, or phone 314-622-4185 and leave a message with the same details.

Bring proof of value: a purchase contract, an appraisal by an appraiser, sales of similar houses, photos of defects, and for rentals the income and expense figures.

  1. Informal review with an appraiser.
  2. Board of Equalization. The request must reach the Assessor by the second Monday in July, and the board sits from July to the last Saturday in August. Ask for the form at that number, by email, or at Room 120 in City Hall.
  3. State Tax Commission. The deadline is September 30 or 30 days after the board rules, whichever comes later. The commission wants a board appeal first, though newly bought property is one of a few exceptions.

A homeowner may represent themselves before the Commission. A commercial owner needs counsel. Under RSMo 138.060, the assessor's number carries no built-in presumption of accuracy, and for a city outside any county the assessor has to show that the value is no higher than market. If you pay while disputing, read RSMo 139.031 first.

The city files a suit, and the sale follows roughly twelve months later. The Sheriff's Office conducts the auction. A notice of each suit is published weekly, and the Collector posts a suit and sale schedule.

An owner can pay the suit in full or call 622-4101 about a Redemption Contract. Opening bids equal the amount in the sale notice's legal description. State law adds a notice step: RSMo 140.150 directs the collector to mail the recorded owner before delinquent land is advertised, and an owner who never receives the letter still owes the tax.

sections.h2: Relief for older or disabled owners
sections.html:
The state offers the Missouri Property Tax Credit Claim, which helps qualified seniors and people who are 100 percent disabled recoup part of the real estate tax or rent they paid. The ceiling is $1,100 for an owner who lives in the home and $750 for a renter, scaled to taxes or rent paid against household income. The state number is (573) 751-3505.

Tax-exempt status is a different track. The Assessor reviews each parcel, and the owner has to present convincing evidence that the use fits Article X, Section 6 of the Missouri Constitution and RSMo 137.100.

sections.h2: Selling a house with tax still due
sections.html:
The balance gets paid out of your proceeds. A title company will search for liens, and a delinquent bill or a pending suit has to be cleared before the buyer can take clean title. Hand over the parcel number early so a payoff figure can be requested.

The Assessor's site also links to the Housing Conservation inspection for residential occupancy, a basic check for minimal interior code violations and minimum exterior standards. Ask the city whether that inspection touches your sale.

Before you list, collect the paperwork a title company will want: your parcel number, the latest tax bill, your loan payoff and any notice you have received from the Collector. If the bill was mailed to a lender or to an old address, check with the Assessor so the record shows where you can be reached. Ask for the payoff figure a few days before closing, because interest keeps building and the amount can change.

A cash buyer can close without a lender's appraisal, which may help if a suit has been filed and time is short, but the tax still has to be cleared through the Collector either way.

faqs.q: Whom do I pay for St. Louis real estate tax?
faqs.a: The Collector of Revenue. Pay at 1200 Market Street, Room 109, through PayIt St. Louis, by mail to PO Box 66877, or by phone at (314) 408-6887.

faqs.q: What does a late bill cost?
faqs.a: One 2% penalty plus 2% interest every month, up to 18% a year, on the balance left after December 31. The interest keeps adding yearly until the account is paid.

faqs.q: Which dates matter for a value appeal?
faqs.a: Informal hearings run May 1 to June 23, and the Board of Equalization request is due the second Monday in July. Email appeal@stlouis-mo.gov or call 314-622-4185 to start.

faqs.q: Does the city have a county treasurer?
faqs.a: No. St. Louis belongs to no county, so the city Assessor and the city Collector of Revenue perform the work a county assessor and collector would elsewhere.

faqs.q: May I close on a sale while tax is overdue?
faqs.a: Yes. The unpaid amount comes out of the proceeds at the table, and the title company can request a payoff. After a suit is filed, the Collector at 622-4101 can discuss a Redemption Contract.
